Original source account: The source describes finite volume methods as using approximate integrals or averages over grid cells, with a cell average equal to the cell integral divided by its volume. These values change at each time step through cell-edge fluxes, and numerical flux functions are constructed from approximate cell averages to approximate the physical fluxes reasonably well [printed page 5, Section 1.2]. The inherited physical balance states that the time derivative of the conserved amount between two endpoints equals the flux at the first endpoint minus the flux at the second [printed page 4, equation (1.10)]. Integral conservation remains applicable at discontinuities even when the differential equation does not hold classically [printed page 5, Section 1.1.2]. The selected numerical description provides no specific update formula, stencil, or quantitative approximation bound [printed page 5, Section 1.2]. assumptions: The governing conservation law has integral form (1.10), with change in the conserved amount accounted for by endpoint fluxes [printed page 4, equation (1.10) and its explanation; printed page 5, Section 1.2, explicit reference to (1.10)].
The domain is divided into grid cells, and approximate cell averages supply the data for determining numerical fluxes [printed page 5, Section 1.2, first paragraph].

Sufficient smoothness is a condition for deriving the differential equation from the integral equation; it is not imposed in the selected paragraph as a requirement for finite volume treatment of discontinuous solutions [printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2; printed page 5, Section 1.2].

The selected description concerns conserved quantities governed by the displayed balance without source terms. The source separately notes that nonconserved quantities require source terms [printed page 4, paragraph following (1.10)].

The finite volume discussion is motivated by accurate approximation of discontinuous solutions, for which classical finite difference methods can break down near discontinuities [printed page 5, Section 1.2, opening sentences].
